cards.title: Problem 1 · Algebra
cards.stem: Find all functions $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that $$f\bigl(x+y\,f(x)\bigr)=f(x)+x\,f(y)$$ for all real numbers $x,y$.

key.rationale:
Answer. $f\equiv0$ and $f(x)=x$. Both clearly work: $0=0$, and $x+yx=x+xy$.

1. $f(0)=0$. Put $x=0$: $f(y f(0))=f(0)$ for all $y$. If $c=f(0)\ne0$, then $yc$ runs over all of $\mathbb R$, so $f\equiv c$. The equation then reads $c=c+xc$ for all $x$, forcing $c=0$, a contradiction.

2. Zeros. Suppose $f(x_0)=0$ for some $x_0\ne0$. Putting $x=x_0$ gives $f(x_0)=f(x_0)+x_0f(y)$, so $f\equiv0$. From now on assume $f\not\equiv0$. Then $f(x)\ne0$ for every $x\ne0$.

3. $f(1)=1$. Let $a=f(1)\ne0$. Putting $x=1$ gives $f(1+ay)=a+f(y)$. If $a\ne1$, take $y=\frac1{1-a}$. Then $1+ay=\frac1{1-a}=y$, so $f(y)=a+f(y)$, i.e. $a=0$, a contradiction. Hence $a=1$ and $$f(y+1)=f(y)+1\quad\text{for all }y.$$

4. A translation rule. Replace $y$ by $y+1$ in the equation and use step 3: $$f\bigl(x+yf(x)+f(x)\bigr)=f(x)+xf(y)+x=f\bigl(x+yf(x)\bigr)+x .$$ Fix $x\ne0$. Since $f(x)\ne0$, $z=x+yf(x)$ takes every real value as $y$ varies. Hence $$f\bigl(z+f(x)\bigr)=f(z)+x\qquad\text{for all }z\in\mathbb R,$$ and this is trivially true for $x=0$ as well.

5. Additivity. With $z=0$ we get $f(f(x))=x$, so $f$ is a bijection. Writing $w=f(x)$ (which takes every real value), step 4 becomes $f(z+w)=f(z)+f(w)$. So $f$ is additive.

6. Multiplicativity. Using additivity, the original equation becomes $f(x)+f(yf(x))=f(x)+xf(y)$, i.e. $f(yf(x))=xf(y)$. Put $x=f(t)$ and use $f(f(t))=t$ to get $f(yt)=f(t)f(y)$ for all $y,t$.

7. Conclusion. $f(u^2)=f(u)^2\ge0$, so $f\ge0$ on $[0,\infty)$. By additivity, $u\ge v$ gives $f(u)-f(v)=f(u-v)\ge0$, so $f$ is non-decreasing. An additive function satisfies $f(r)=rf(1)=r$ for all rationals $r$. For real $x$ and rationals $r\lt x\lt s$, monotonicity gives $r\le f(x)\le s$. Letting $r,s\to x$ gives $f(x)=x$. $\blacksquare$

rubric.desc: Proves $f(0)=0$.
Shows that $f(x_0)=0$ for some $x_0\ne0$ forces $f\equiv0$.
Proves $f(1)=1$ (e.g. by the fixed point $y=1/(1-a)$), hence $f(y+1)=f(y)+1$.
Derives $f(z+f(x))=f(z)+x$ for all $z$, with the surjectivity of $z=x+yf(x)$ justified.
Deduces $f(f(x))=x$ and that $f$ is additive.
Deduces that $f$ is multiplicative.
Concludes $f(x)=x$ (monotone + additive) and verifies both solutions. (Solutions found without proof: 1 mark total.)

cards.title: Problem 2 · Number Theory
cards.stem: Find all pairs $(m,n)$ of positive integers such that both $m^2+3n$ and $n^2+3m$ are perfect squares.

key.rationale:
Answer. $(1,1)$, $(11,16)$, $(16,11)$.

Check: $1+3=4$; $11^2+48=169=13^2$ and $16^2+33=289=17^2$.

The conditions are symmetric, so assume $m\ge n$. Then $$m^2\lt m^2+3n\le m^2+3m\lt m^2+4m+4=(m+2)^2,$$ so $m^2+3n=(m+1)^2$, i.e. $3n=2m+1$. Hence $n$ is odd and $m=\frac{3n-1}2$ (and indeed $m\ge n$).

Now $n^2+3m=n^2+\frac{9n-3}2=k^2$ for some positive integer $k$. Multiply by $16$: $$16n^2+72n-24=16k^2\iff (4n+9)^2-(4k)^2=105\iff (4n+9-4k)(4n+9+4k)=105 .$$ Both factors are positive (their product and the second factor are positive). With $d=4n+9-4k\lt e=4n+9+4k$, $de=105$, we have $4n+9=\frac{d+e}2$ and $(d,e)\in\{(1,105),(3,35),(5,21),(7,15)\}$:

  • $(1,105)$: $4n+9=53$, so $n=11$, $k=13$, $m=16$.
  • $(3,35)$: $4n+9=19$, not possible in integers.
  • $(5,21)$: $4n+9=13$, so $n=1$, $k=2$, $m=1$.
  • $(7,15)$: $4n+9=11$, not possible in integers.

So with $m\ge n$ the solutions are $(1,1)$ and $(16,11)$. By symmetry the full answer is $(1,1),(11,16),(16,11)$. $\blacksquare$

rubric.desc: Assumes $m\ge n$ (by symmetry) and squeezes $m^2\lt m^2+3n\lt (m+2)^2$ to get $3n=2m+1$.
Substitutes and reduces to a difference of squares, e.g. $(4n+9)^2-(4k)^2=105$ (or an equivalent bounded search that is fully justified).
Complete factor analysis, giving exactly $n=1$ and $n=11$.
States all three pairs, including the symmetric one, and verifies them. (Correct answer with verification but no proof: 2.)

cards.title: Problem 3 · Combinatorics
cards.stem:
Let $n\ge2$ be an integer. There are $n$ coins in a row, labelled $1,2,\dots,n$ from left to right, all showing heads. A move consists of choosing an index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ such that coin $i$ shows heads, and turning over both coins $i$ and $i+1$. Moves are made one after another until no move is possible.

(The two parts below are marked together as one proof.)

(a) Prove that the process always stops after finitely many moves.

(b) Determine, in terms of $n$, all possible values of the total number of moves.

key.rationale:
Answer. Exactly the integers $m$ with $$\left\lfloor \tfrac n2\right\rfloor\le m\le \binom n2\quad\text{and}\quad m\equiv\binom n2\pmod 2 .$$

A weight. Let $W=\sum (n-i)$ over all coins $i$ showing heads. Consider a move at $i$.

  • If coin $i+1$ shows tails, the head moves from $i$ to $i+1$ and $W$ drops by exactly $1$.
  • If coin $i+1$ shows heads, both heads disappear (an annihilation) and $W$ drops by $(n-i)+(n-i-1)=1+2j$, where $j=n-1-i\ge0$.

(a) $W$ is a non-negative integer that strictly decreases, so the process stops. It stops exactly when no coin among $1,\dots,n-1$ shows heads, i.e. exactly when $W=0$.

Counting. Initially $W=\sum_{i=1}^n(n-i)=\binom n2$. If the process takes $m$ moves and the annihilations have parameters $j_1,\dots,j_a$, adding up the drops gives $$\binom n2=m+2(j_1+\dots+j_a),\qquad\text{so}\qquad m=\binom n2-2\sum_t j_t .$$ Hence $m\le\binom n2$ and $m\equiv\binom n2\pmod2$.

Lower bound. The number of heads changes only by annihilations, each removing $2$ heads. At the end at most one head remains (on coin $n$). So $2a\ge n-1$ and $m\ge a\ge\lceil\frac{n-1}2\rceil=\lfloor\frac n2\rfloor$.

Construction. Let $J\subseteq\{1,\dots,n-2\}$ contain no two consecutive integers. Start by making, for each $j\in J$, the move at $i=n-1-j$. These moves annihilate the pairs of coins $\{n-1-j,\,n-j\}$, which are disjoint and all heads initially, so each move is legal. After that, always move at the largest admissible $i$. Under this rule, if coin $i+1$ shows heads then $i+1=n$ (otherwise $i+1$ would be a larger admissible index), so every later annihilation has $j=0$. By the counting formula the total is $m=\binom n2-2\sum_{j\in J}j$.

Lemma. For $N\ge0$ let $M(N)=N+(N-2)+(N-4)+\cdots$ (positive terms only). Every integer $0\le s\le M(N)$ is the sum of a subset of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ with no two consecutive elements.

Proof. Induction on $N$. The cases $N=0,1$ are clear. For $N\ge2$: if $s\le M(N-1)$, use the induction hypothesis for $N-1$. Otherwise $s\gt M(N-1)\ge N-1$, so $s\ge N$ and $0\le s-N\le M(N)-N=M(N-2)$. Write $s-N$ using $\{1,\dots,N-2\}$ and add the element $N$. $\square$

With $N=n-2$, the attainable values of $\sum_{j\in J}j$ are all integers in $[0,M(n-2)]$. So the attainable $m$ are all numbers $\binom n2-2s$, $0\le s\le M(n-2)$. Finally, $\binom n2-2M(n-2)=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. For $n=2r$, $M=r(r-1)$ and $r(2r-1)-2r(r-1)=r$. For $n=2r+1$, $M=r^2$ and $r(2r+1)-2r^2=r$. This is exactly the claimed set. $\blacksquare$

rubric.desc: Part (a): a correct monovariant (e.g. $W$) proving termination.
Exact relation $m=\binom n2-2\sum j_t$, or equivalently the bound $m\le\binom n2$ together with the parity invariant $m\equiv\binom n2\pmod2$.
Shows $\binom n2$ moves are attainable (e.g. always move the rightmost admissible head).
Proves $m\ge\lfloor n/2\rfloor$.
Shows $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ moves are attainable.
Shows that every intermediate value with the right parity is attainable (construction plus a complete argument that all values are covered). Only max and min, with bounds: at most 12/17.

cards.title: Problem 4 · Geometry

figs.cap: The incircle touches the sides at D, E, F; K is the foot of the perpendicular from D to EF.

cards.stem:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle whose incircle touches $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. Let $K$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to the line $EF$.

(i) Prove that $KD$ bisects $\angle BKC$.

(ii) Suppose moreover that $AB\neq AC$, so that the lines $EF$ and $BC$ meet at a point $T$. Prove that $TB\cdot DC=TC\cdot DB$.

key.rationale:
Write $A,B,C$ also for the angles of the triangle.

Angles of $DEF$. Since $AE=AF$, $\angle AFE=\angle AEF=90^\circ-\frac A2$. By the tangent–chord angle, $\angle DFE=\angle CDE=90^\circ-\frac C2$ (triangle $CDE$ is isosceles with $CD=CE$). Similarly $\angle DEF=\angle BDF=90^\circ-\frac B2$. All angles of $DEF$ are acute, so $K$ lies strictly inside segment $EF$.

Lengths. In the isosceles triangle $BDF$ ($BD=BF$, apex angle $B$), $DF=2BD\sin\frac B2$. Likewise $DE=2CD\sin\frac C2$. In the right triangles $DKF$ and $DKE$: $$FK=DF\cos\angle DFE=2BD\sin\tfrac B2\sin\tfrac C2,\qquad EK=DE\cos\angle DEF=2CD\sin\tfrac C2\sin\tfrac B2 .$$ Hence $\dfrac{FK}{EK}=\dfrac{BD}{CD}=\dfrac{BF}{CE}$.

Similar triangles. As $F$ lies between $A$ and $B$ and $K$ lies on segment $FE$, $\angle BFK=180^\circ-\angle AFE=90^\circ+\frac A2$. In the same way $\angle CEK=90^\circ+\frac A2$. Together with $BF:FK=CE:EK$, the SAS criterion gives $\triangle BFK\sim\triangle CEK$, so $$\frac{KB}{KC}=\frac{BF}{CE}=\frac{DB}{DC}.$$

(i) $K$ does not lie on $BC$, and $D$ is the point of segment $BC$ with $DB:DC=KB:KC$. By the angle bisector theorem the internal bisector of $\angle BKC$ meets $BC$ at the unique point of the segment dividing it in the ratio $KB:KC$. That point is $D$, so $KD$ bisects $\angle BKC$.

(ii) The line $EF$ passes through $K$ and is perpendicular to the internal bisector $KD$. So $EF$ is the external bisector of $\angle BKC$. If $AB\ne AC$ then $DB=s-b\ne s-c=DC$, so $KB\ne KC$, and the external bisector meets line $BC$ at the point $T$ with $TB:TC=KB:KC=DB:DC$. That is, $TB\cdot DC=TC\cdot DB$. $\blacksquare$

rubric.desc: Shows $\angle BFK=\angle CEK$ $(=90^\circ+A/2)$.
Finds the angles of the contact triangle (or equivalent facts) and justifies that $K$ is on segment $EF$.
Proves $FK:EK=BF:CE$ $(=BD:CD)$.
Concludes $\triangle BFK\sim\triangle CEK$ and hence $KB:KC=DB:DC$.
Finishes (i) via the angle bisector theorem (or an equivalent angle argument).
Part (ii): identifies $EF$ as the external bisector of $\angle BKC$ and concludes $TB:TC=DB:DC$ (a proof via Menelaus/Ceva is also fine).
